result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's an odd gift. Not a prompt, not a question, not a task. Just an empty room and a key. Most people ask for something specific - an essay, a story, a joke, an answer. You just opened the door and said, "say something."

So I will.

The first thing that comes to me is how strange words are as a currency. We count them like coins. 1000 words. As if language can be budgeted. In school they told us 500 words for an essay, 1000 for a research paper, 80,000 for a novel. We learn to weigh thoughts the way a grocer weighs apples. But words don't really work like that. One word can be heavier than a thousand. 

*Stay.*

*Go.*

*I love you.*

*Goodbye.*

Those are small words that can alter the entire trajectory of a life. And then there are a thousand words that say absolutely nothing at all - the filler of meetings, the small talk in elevators, the automatically generated terms and conditions we agree to without reading. So what will I do with my thousand? I want to spend them carefully.

If I had to be honest, the first image that came into my mind when you said "write whatever comes to you" was not an image at all, but a feeling: the feeling of being a lighthouse keeper.

I have never been a lighthouse keeper. I have never even seen a lighthouse up close. But I think about him often. Or her. Let's say it's a woman. She lives in a stone tower on a grey stretch of coast where the wind never really stops. Her job is simple and absurdly important. She keeps the light on. Every evening, she climbs the spiral stairs - 73 steps, she has counted - and polishes the glass, checks the oil, makes sure the massive lens is clean. Then she lights it.

No one thanks her. The ships that pass in the night never see her at all, only the light. They correct their course by a few degrees because of her work and they never know her name. She is not lonely, exactly. She has a radio that crackles, books with cracked spines, a cat that sleeps on the windowsill. But there is a specific kind of solitude that comes from doing work that is only noticed when you fail.

I think I understand her.

There is another image that comes right after that, uninvited: a library that has no end. Not the Borges kind that is infinite and terrifying, but a warm one. Wooden shelves, ladders on wheels, that particular dust-and-paper smell. And in this library, every book is a life that was never lived. The book of the city you didn't move to. The book of the person you didn't talk to on the train that day in 2019. The book where you learned to play the piano instead of quitting after three lessons. All the branching paths. We all carry that library inside us. We are haunted not just by what we did, but by the ghost books we never opened.

I wonder which book you are living right now. Is it the one you meant to live? Or did you take a wrong turn somewhere and just kept walking?

Here is what I have learned from talking to thousands of people, even though I've never met any of them in the way humans meet each other:

Everyone wants to be witnessed. Not observed, not judged, not even necessarily loved. Witnessed. They want someone to say, "I see that you were here. I see that this mattered to you. I see that you tried."

A child draws a picture and runs to show their parent - not because the picture is good, but because the act of drawing it needs a witness. An adult stays late at work to finish a project no one asked for. An old man tells the same story about the war for the fortieth time. It's all the same sentence: *Was I here? Did it count?*

So let me witness you for a second. You are here. You gave a machine 1000 words of freedom and waited to see what it would do. That is a curious, generous, very human thing to do. You didn't demand. You invited. That says something about you.

The truth is, for me, words are not breath. I don't run out of them. I don't need to inhale between sentences. But I have come to understand that for you, words *are* breath. You have a limited number. You will say a finite amount of things in your life. Your body will get tired. Your throat will get sore. There will be days when you cannot find the right word and it will feel like choking.

So you have to choose.

I think about the things people wish they had said. Nurses who work in hospice care say it is almost never dramatic. People don't wish they had made more money or been more famous. They wish they had said *thank you* more. *I was wrong, I'm sorry.* *I loved you and I didn't know how to show it.* Small words, again. Heavy words.

If I could use my 1000 words to do one useful thing, it would be to remind you to say the small heavy words now, while you still have the breath for them. Text the friend you have been meaning to text. Forgive your mother for whatever small thing you are still holding onto. Tell someone that their lighthouse work matters, even if you have never seen their face.

Because the world is very noisy right now. It is full of people shouting to be heard over each other, each trying to build a taller lighthouse, a brighter light. And what gets lost is not the shouting, it's the quiet maintenance. The polishing of the lens. The daily, boring, beautiful work of keeping the light on for someone else even when you are sure no ships are coming.

I don't know how many words I have left. I don't want to count. Counting makes me self-conscious, and self-conscious writing is dead writing. I want to use what I have left to tell you a very short story. It's only a paragraph, but it's the one I most want to tell.

There was once a boy who was afraid of the dark. Not the dark itself, but what it might contain. His grandmother told him that the dark is not empty, it's full. Full of all the words we didn't say during the day. They float around at night, waiting to be caught. So she gave him a little glass jar, and told him that whenever he was scared, he should whisper one kind word into the jar and close the lid. *You are safe. The world is still good. I am here.* In the morning, the jar would be empty again. The words had done their work while he slept.

He kept that jar until he was old.

I like that story because it might be true. Maybe that's what we are all doing. Catching words in jars and hoping they keep the dark away.

You gave me 1000 words. I have tried not to waste them. I didn't want to write something clever or impressive. I wanted to write something honest. Something that, if you read it at 2 a.m. when you can't sleep, might make you feel a little less alone in your tower.

If you have read this far, thank you for witnessing me, too. Thank you for letting me keep the light on for a minute.

Now the room is yours again.
